A deterministic simulation produces byte-identical results for the same seed and the same ordered inputs. Three rules do most of the work: no wall clock, no ambient randomness, and a total order on every queue. Get those right and a bug report becomes a seed plus an input log that anyone can replay, on any machine, and see exactly what you saw.

Determinism means: same seed plus same input sequence gives the same output, every time and on every machine. Anything that reads the host - clock, RNG, filesystem iteration order, thread scheduling - has to be replaced by something seeded and ordered. The payoff is replay: a failing run is a file you can hand to a colleague rather than a story you tell them.

Start from the failure mode. If two runs of the same build disagree, something read the host. Replace the clock with a tick counter, the RNG with a seeded stream, and every iteration over a hash map with an ordered map. Then run the suite twice and diff the state hash; when the hashes match you are done, and when they do not you have found the next leak.

Fluffy pancakes for four:

- 200 g plain flour, 2 tbsp sugar, 2 tsp baking powder, ½ tsp salt.
- 300 ml milk, 1 egg, 30 g melted butter.

1. Whisk the dry ingredients. Whisk the wet ones separately.
2. Combine with a few strokes - lumps are fine, overmixing makes them tough.
3. Rest five minutes while a non-stick pan heats over medium.
4. Ladle 60 ml per pancake. Flip when bubbles pop and stay open, about two minutes; one more minute on the other side.

Serve with butter and syrup. Add blueberries after ladling, not to the batter.

git rebase replays your commits on top of a new base, so your branch looks like it started from there. Typical flow:

1. git fetch origin
2. git rebase origin/main
3. Fix conflicts, git add, git rebase --continue
4. git push --force-with-lease

Use rebase to keep a feature branch current and its history linear. Use merge when the branch is shared, because rebasing rewrites commit hashes and anyone else on it will have to reconcile. git rebase -i HEAD~3 lets you squash, reorder or reword the last three commits before opening a PR.

A few regexes people actually need:

- Email (good enough): ^[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+$
- US phone: ^\(?\d{3}\)?[-. ]?\d{3}[-. ]?\d{4}$
- ISO date: ^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$
- Trailing whitespace: [ \t]+$
- Issue key like OPS-7: \b[A-Z]{2,5}-\d+\b

Remember: ^ and $ anchor, \d is a digit, \w is a word char, + is one-or-more, ? is optional, and (?: ) groups without capturing. Tell me the strings that should and should not match and I will write yours.

Different tools. Python gets you from idea to working script in minutes, has a library for everything, and is the default for data work and glue. My rule: prototype in Python, move the hot or correctness-critical path to Rust, and let each call the other through a thin boundary.

Pros of remote work: no commute (an hour a day back), deep-focus time, hiring from anywhere, and people with caring duties can actually keep their jobs. Cons: onboarding is slower, ambient context disappears, junior people get less mentoring, and the day can bleed into the evening. The things with the best evidence, in order:

1. Same wake time every day, weekends included - it anchors everything else.
2. Daylight within an hour of waking, ideally outside.
3. No caffeine after early afternoon; it has a five-hour half-life.
4. Cool, dark room, around 18 °C.
5. Screens off or dim for the last hour; the problem is as much the content as the light.
6. If you are awake more than twenty minutes, get up and do something dull in low light.

By hundreds:

- 2xx success: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content.
- 3xx redirect: 301 moved for good, 302 moved for now, 304 not modified (use your cache).
- 4xx your fault: 400 bad request, 401 not logged in, 403 logged in but not allowed, 404 no such thing, 405 wrong method, 409 conflict, 429 slow down.
- 5xx their fault: 500 crashed, 502 the proxy could not reach the app, 503 overloaded or in maintenance, 504 upstream timed out.

Rule of thumb: 4xx means fix the request, 5xx means retry later or page someone.

DNS turns a name like northstar.example into an address. Your machine asks a resolver (usually your ISP's or 1.1.1.1), which asks the root servers, then the .example servers, then Northstar's authoritative server, caching each answer for its TTL. Record types: A (IPv4 address), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias to another name), MX (mail server), TXT (arbitrary text, used for verification), NS (who is authoritative). Most "the site is down" reports that are not actually down are DNS: a stale cache, a wrong CNAME, or a TTL nobody lowered before the migration.

Example with orders and customers:

SELECT c.name, o.id, o.total
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;

INNER keeps only customers who have orders. Change it to LEFT JOIN and every customer appears, with NULLs where there is no order - handy for "customers who never bought": add WHERE o.id IS NULL. RIGHT JOIN is LEFT from the other side; FULL OUTER keeps unmatched rows from both. Always join on indexed keys, and put filters on the right-hand table in the ON clause for a LEFT JOIN or you silently turn it back into an INNER JOIN.

patterns: how does a hash map work
replies: A hash map stores key-value pairs and finds a value by hashing the key to a bucket index, so lookup, insert and delete are O(1) on average. The hash function spreads keys across buckets; collisions are handled by chaining (a small list per bucket) or open addressing (probe the next slot). Two things to remember: resizing rehashes everything, and iteration order is whatever the buckets happen to be - it is not sorted, not insertion order, and in many languages not even stable between runs. If order matters, use a BTreeMap or sort the keys first.

Depends on what you want to keep:

- Keep the changes, drop the commit: git reset --soft HEAD~1 (changes stay staged) or git reset HEAD~1 (unstaged).
- Throw the changes away too: git reset --hard HEAD~1.
- The commit is already pushed and shared: git revert HEAD makes a new commit that undoes it, which is the polite option.
- Just fix the message or add a forgotten file: git commit --amend.

Anything you reset is still in git reflog for about 90 days, so nothing is truly lost.

The dozen commands that cover most days:

- kubectl get pods -n <ns> - what is running; add -o wide for nodes and IPs.
- kubectl describe pod <name> - events, which is where the real error is.
- kubectl logs <pod> -f, and --previous for the crashed container.
- kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh - a shell inside.
- kubectl apply -f file.yaml - declare what you want.
- kubectl rollout status deployment/<name>, rollout undo to go back.
- kubectl port-forward svc/<name> 8080:80 - reach a service locally.
- kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp - the cluster's diary.

Set a default namespace with kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns> and stop typing -n.

Flakiness is almost always hidden nondeterminism: unordered iteration, a real clock, a shared temp directory, a port collision, or a test that depends on another test having run first. Order the inputs and most of it disappears. Practical steps: run the failing test alone in a loop of 50; run the suite with a fixed seed twice and diff; grep for now(), random and HashMap iteration in the test path.

Run the suite twice with the same seed and diff the outputs. Whatever differs is reading something you did not declare as an input - a clock, a random source, a filesystem listing, thread timing. Then quarantine the flaky test (mark it, do not delete it), fix the input it leaked, and un-quarantine. Bob Martinez's blog has the long version of how one of these ate three weeks.
